en: Abhidhānottara 7 = Palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Now I shall further describe the mandala, the supreme commitment (samaya),
the secret and esoteric ground of all desires that bestows accomplishment.
For the benefit of practitioners, I shall reveal this oral tradition.

In the center of the eastern maṇḍala, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus endowed with filaments of every color, which bestows the fruit of all desires. In its center, one should visualize the syllable HŪṂ as Vajrasattva.
Complete with all the primary marks and adorned with the secondary characteristics,
it is the supreme non-duality arising from the union of great passion;
it has the form of the flowing bodhicitta, as stainless as the moon of awakening.
The goddess, arisen from its rays, should be exhorted with this song:

HŪṂ RAMA RAMA HOḤ! Great bliss, great bliss, with the essence of passion, HO PAI-AJJU ALALALA HOḤ! Supreme great bliss, understand this through the act of union; O Blessed One, Greatly Satisfied, OṂ VAJRASATTVA SURATASTVA.
In the presence of the supreme great passion of all essences, may the supreme essence, the delight of all *rāmās*, and all *yoginīs* attain accomplishment! Hoḥ! O Blessed One, Great Vajra-Lover, Hūṃ!
Alala la hoḥ! O Blessed One, Great Passion of Passionate Love, who are you? Delight me; sport with me in the *saṃvara-padmā*.

Alalala hoḥ! O excellent Vajra, O one with a face as pleasant as a mass of lotuses, O you whose face is naturally smiling! O supreme lotus-like jewel, may you strike the staff of ignorance with the blow of the sun; O supreme Vajra, O sweet nectar of the gods, may the assembly of the gods be rendered languid; O today’s [disciple], may you attain the awakening that is difficult to reach. Alalala hoḥ! O you who have turned toward the commitment! Alalala hoḥ! O great jewel, O incomparable one!
Immediately after this song was sung,
they remained standing right there and gazed upon the Blessed One, Śrī Samvaravajra, together with his assembly—
the Blessed One who has four faces, with blue, yellow, red, and green countenances.

He has three eyes and twelve arms; he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with the soles of his feet treading upon Mahābhairava and Kālarātri; at the time of the commitment (*samaya*), he embraces Vajravārāhī with two arms holding a vajra and bell, while the other two arms wear the hide of Gaṇapati as a garment.
In the third right hand he holds a ḍamaru drum, in the fourth an axe,
in the fifth a scimitar, and in the sixth a raised vajra-spear.

In the third left arm he holds a vajra-khaṭvāṅga, in the fourth a skull-cup filled with nectar, in the fifth a vajra-noose, and in the sixth the head of one of the four Māras; he is adorned with a crown of matted locks,
topped with a crest of garlands of skulls and bearing the crescent moon, his head-dress being marked by a double-vajra.
With a distorted face, terrifying with prominent fangs, imbued with the sentiments of erotic love and the rest,
clad in a tiger skin, wearing a garland of human heads,
and adorned with necklaces, bracelets, earrings, and a crest-jewel;
The sacred thread, and the ashes—these are proclaimed as the six mudrās.

In front of him is the Blessed Lady Samaya-Vajravārāhī, of the same color [as him], with one face, two arms, and three eyes; her hair is loose, she is naked, and she wears a girdle adorned with bone fragments.
Her left arm embraces [the consort] while holding a skull-cup filled with the blood of wicked Māras, and in her right hand she holds a threatening gesture (tarjanī) and a flaying knife (kartṛkā).
Possessing great splendor like the fire at the end of an eon, they flow forth, being fond of blood.
She is coiled around the two thighs, her nature consisting of great bliss and compassion.
Arising from Āli and Kāli, it is the impurity of the method of all phenomena.
The Goddess, who bestows all accomplishments, transcends the reality of the two kalpas and is free from both dharma and adharma; she should be placed upon the petals of the lotus—
black, yellow, red, and green, possessing a fierce form.
All [the goddesses] have three faces, six arms, three eyes, and stand in the *ālīḍha* posture;
they are naked, with disheveled hair, and equal in size to the four Māras;
they are intensely impassioned by passion and utterly intoxicated.
She wears a crown of garlands of skulls, is adorned with the five mudrās, and is black, yellow, and green, terrifying with her squinting eyes.
The Father is black and green, filled with the aesthetic flavor of compassion (karuṇa-rasa);

the Mother is red, black, and green, manifesting the grace of the erotic flavor (śṛṅgāra-rasa); and the [other] faces are green, black, and white, displaying the flavors of laughter, wrath, and terror.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga; in her right hands are a hand-drum and a curved knife, and likewise a severed head and a vajra-spear in her left and right hands respectively.
In the intermediate directions, however, are the four Karuṇās.
The vessels containing the bodhicitta and other substances are filled with the water of the five nectars and placed at the mouth.
The goddesses beginning with Kākāsyā stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture;
they are black, dark, red, and fair-complexioned respectively, each having one face and four arms.
They possess three eyes, have fierce forms, and are resplendent with disheveled hair.

Wearing a crown of garlands of skulls and adorned with the five mudrās, they are naked, mounted upon corpses, and overwhelmed by compassion and desire. In their left hands they hold a severed head and a khaṭvāṅga staff; in their right hands they hold a skull-cup and a flaying knife.
In the intermediate directions, however, are the four *ḍākinīs*, Yamadāḍhī and the others;
they have four arms and one face, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture,
rest upon the backs of *pretas*, possess three eyes, have disheveled hair, and are terrifying.
They wear crowns of garlands of skulls and are sealed with the five mudrās;
they are naked, possessing universal forms, and are agitated by throbbing, eager intensity.
In their left hands they hold skull-cups and khaṭvāṅgas, and in their right hands they hold hand-drums and flaying knives.
Placed counter-clockwise, they grant accomplishment in the intermediate directions;
likewise, Kākāsyā is placed at the door clockwise.
This is the meditation on the elements, aggregates, sense-bases, and the body, speech, and mind.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the previously stated sequence and in accordance with the rules,
one should place therein— in the center— the four elements beginning with earth, namely the spheres of Indra (earth), Varuṇa (water), Agni (fire), and Vāyu (air).
Pātanī, Māraṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, and likewise Nartanī;
the element of space (ākāśadhātu) is therein Padmajālinī Śūnyatā.
Having perceived Vairocana in form, and Vajrasūrya in sensation. [49.2]
In perception (*saṃjñā*), he is King Īśvara; in formative factors (*saṃskāra*), he is the two Vajrarājas;
in consciousness (*vijñāna*), he is Vajrasattva; and in the state of all Tathāgatas, he is Śrī Heruka.
In the eye, he is Mohavajra; and in the ear, he is the two forms of Dveṣavajra.
In the nose is Īrṣyāvajra, and in the mouth indeed are Rāgavajra and [Dveṣavajra];
in touch is Mātsaryavajra, and in all the sense-bases is Aiśvaryavajra.
In the mind there should be the *hūṃ*-syllable vajra; the syllable *āḥ* should be speech;
the syllable *oṃ* is the body-vajra, while the syllable *he* belongs to the two wisdom-vajras.
Through the yoga of sequence in the assembly, one should meditate with one's entire being.
O Blessed One, the twelfth is the one who is impassioned by the passion for bliss.
Then, having beheld the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra), one should satisfy it with offerings, praises, and so forth;
having entered the yoga of passion, one should become of one taste (samarasībhavet).
One should meditate through the nature of existence upon the sequential process of emanation and reabsorption.
By means of the yoga of the pledge of worship, one should perform the recitation according to the ritual injunction:
*oṃ vajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasamvara svāhā*. This is the heart mantra.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the near-heart mantra.
Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart and near-heart mantra of Vārāhī.
Oṃ, to the ḍākinī, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ lāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā— one should cause [the mantra] to end thus.
Oṃ kākāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ ulūkāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ, to the dog-faced one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ sūkarāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadāḍhī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadūtī hūṃ phūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadraṣṭriṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā || Oṃ yamamathanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ||
One should meditate upon this supreme meditation through the yoga of withdrawal as a throbbing vibration.
This is the supreme secret, the oral tradition of the Yoginīs,
concerning the Lord of Mantras, the Leader of Mantras, who is complete with the single sixteenth digit.
But at the time of arising from meditation, one should place the two armors.
Oṃ ha; in the heart is Vajrasattva.
Vairocana is indeed on the head.
Svāhā hūṃ: Padmanarteśvara at the crest-lock (śikhā). Vauṣaṭ he: Heruka at the two shoulders.
Hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ: Vajrasūrya at the eyes.
PHAṬ HAṂ: the weapon-mantra in all limbs is Paramāśva.
Oṃ vaṃ at the navel is Vajravārāhī; haṃ yoṃ at the heart is Yāminī;
hrīṃ moṃ at the face is Mohinī.
PHREṂ HRĪṂ: Saṃcālinī at the head.
HŪṂ HŪṂ: Saṃtrāsinī at the crest-lock.
PHAṬ HĀṂ: Caṇḍikā is the weapon for all limbs.
Thus, one should dwell in the abiding in the single equality of all phenomena through the cultivation of the equality of existence.
At the time of the equality of the five wisdoms, the yogin should always cause [the mind] to flow;
he should observe this four times or three times a day, according to his devotion.
This supreme secret should not be told to just anyone.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Vows of the Samaya, in the Abhidhānottara.
